title: Optimizing Quantum Algorithms on Bipotent Architectures
abstract_summary: The paper studies trade-offs between hardware-level gate improvements (direct-CX) and user-side pulse-level optimizations (ECR-CX) on bipotent quantum architectures, using QAOA instances for portfolio optimization and MaxCut as benchmarks. Through experiments on IBM QPUs, the authors show that pulse-level optimizations often yield larger performance gains than improved monolithic gates, and they propose qubit-mapping strategies (bipotent circuits) that balance fidelity, gate type, and schedule duration to enhance algorithm performance.
methodology_description: The authors evaluate trade-offs between hardware-level gate improvements (direct-CX) and algorithm-level, user-side pulse optimizations (ECR-CX with pulse-level optimizations) for QAOA implementations of dense portfolio-optimization (PortOpt) and MaxCut instances on bipotent IBM superconducting QPUs. They (1) collected hourly calibration data for ibmq ehningen (September 2022) to compare gate error rates and schedule durations for direct-CX vs ECR-CX; (2) pre-transpiled QAOA circuits to a linear topology using an exact, scalable mapping approach to minimize depth; (3) defined an Algorithm-Native Gate Set (H, ZZ, ZZ-SWAP, RZ, RX) and focused pulse-level optimizations on frequently occurring two-qubit primitives (ZZ and ZZ-SWAP) when implemented via ECR-CX; (4) constructed several mapping strategies (ECR-only, Direct-only, Global best-fidelity, and Bipotent which trades fidelity, schedule duration and gate type) using Mapomatic and a bipotent selection rule; (5) performed variational parameter optimization with the COBYLA optimizer using Qiskit’s QASM simulator to obtain parameter values and used those parameters to run experiments on hardware; (6) executed experiments on two IBM QPUs (ibmq ehningen and ibm auckland) with 3–5 qubit PortOpt instances and 5-qubit MaxCut, using 50,000 shots per circuit, applying Qiskit default readout mitigation; and (7) measured empirical metrics including Approximation Ratio (AR), Success Probability (SP), schedule durations, CX counts, and process fidelities (via Qiskit quantum process tomography) to compare default vs pulse-optimized implementations and different qubit-selection strategies. The methodology emphasizes pulse-level optimization where available (no additional calibrations) and a controlled comparison across mapping strategies and gate implementations.
experimental_setup: Noiseless parameter optimization performed with Qiskit's QASM simulator (COBYLA optimizer). Hardware experiments executed on IBM cloud QPUs: ibmq ehningen and ibm auckland. Circuits pre-transpiled to a linear topology using an exact mapping method. Shots per circuit: 50,000. Readout error mitigation: Qiskit default.
dataset_used: Portfolio optimization instances transformed to QUBO (3-, 4-, and 5-asset instances based on a referenced 5-asset instance from prior work [44]; PortOpt parameters q, B, A, λ are specified per instance). Also MaxCut on the complete 5-node graph (dense connectivity).

experiment_input.PortOpt_source: five-asset PortOpt instance from prior work (reference [44])
experiment_input.preprocessing: Classical transformation of PortOpt to QUBO, mapping QUBO to quantum ZZ/Pauli-Z operators; circuits pre-transpiled to linear topology (exact method [33])
experiment_input.notes: For hardware runs, QAOA variational parameters were obtained with COBYLA using Qiskit's QASM simulator and then applied on QPUs.

steps: Collect hourly calibration data (CX error rates, durations, T1/T2, readout errors) for ibmq ehningen.
Pre-transpile QAOA circuits to linear topology using an exact and scalable mapping approach that minimizes depth.
Construct Algorithm-Native Gate Set (H, ZZ, ZZ-SWAP, RZ, RX) and identify two-qubit primitives to optimize.

Generate multiple qubit-mapping strategies: ECR-only (use only ECR-CX links), Direct-only (use only direct-CX links), Global (best-fidelity linear arrangement regardless of CX type), and Bipotent (select qubit linears trading fidelity, schedule duration, and requiring at least one ECR and one direct link). Use Mapomatic for fidelity-based arrangements.

Apply pulse-level optimizations where available: ZZOPT (optimized ZZ implemented via ECR-CX with reduced CR pulses) and ZZ-SWAPOPT (decompose ZZ-SWAP into CZ gates and apply CZOPT pulse optimization). Do not perform additional calibrations.
Optimize variational parameters (QAOA angles) with COBYLA on Qiskit QASM simulator to get parameter sets (p in {1..5}).
Execute compiled circuits on QPUs (ibmq ehningen and ibm auckland) with 50,000 shots per circuit; apply Qiskit default readout error mitigation.

Measure metrics: AR, SP, schedule duration, CX gate count. Run quantum process tomography (QPT, Qiskit standard) for selected two-qubit primitives to compute process fidelity/infidelity as function of rotation angle and repetition counts.
experiment_process.tools_used: Qiskit (circuit construction, pulse-level transpilation, QASM simulator, QPT), Mapomatic (qubit-selection), custom mapping [33]

measured_metrics: Schedule duration (total circuit execution time in nanoseconds/µs)
Process fidelity / infidelity from quantum process tomography for two-qubit gates
experiment_output.baselines: Noiseless QASM-simulator results for AR and SP used as baseline (tables of simulated AR/SP for PortOpt and MaxCut). Comparisons across mapping strategies and with/without pulse-level optimizations.
experiment_output.output_format: Per-instance and per-p (1..5) numeric metrics plotted and tabulated (AR, SP, schedule duration, CX count). Process fidelity plots vs rotation angle and repetition.

gate_types_evaluated: direct-CX (shorter duration, better calibrated but no user pulse optimization without extra calibration)
pulse_optimizations: ZZ-SWAPOPT (ZZ-SWAP decomposed to CZ and pulse-optimized CZOPT)
experiment_parameters.pretranspile_method: Exact, scalable linear mapping minimizing depth (reference [33])
qubit_selection_strategies: Bipotent selection (trade-off fidelity + schedule duration + require at least one ECR and one direct link)

hardware_details.notes: ibmq ehningen is a 27-qubit device with a bipotent architecture (some links provide direct-CX, some ECR-CX). Calibration snapshots collected hourly in September 2022. ibm auckland has a similar bipotent layout.

reproducibility_notes: The authors used Qiskit (including Qiskit Pulse/OpenPulse and the QASM simulator), Mapomatic for fidelity-based mapping, and an exact linear pre-transpilation method referenced as [33]. Variational parameter optimization used COBYLA on the QASM simulator; hardware experiments used the optimized angles with 50,000 shots. Process tomography and process-fidelity computations used standard Qiskit implementations. The paper provides per-instance PortOpt parameters and indicates the specific qubit sets used for each experimental condition, plus calibration snapshots summarized in appendices. However, no public repository or code link is provided in the text; reproducing results would require access to the same (or contemporaneous) IBM calibration data and reimplementation of mapping/pre-transpilation and pulse-optimization steps using Qiskit and Mapomatic. Thus reproducibility is feasible in principle but requires reconstruction of their pipelines and access to IBM hardware and (time-matched) calibration data.
key_findings: [supported] On bipotent IBM superconducting QPUs studied (ibmq ehningen and ibm auckland), applying pulse-level optimizations (ZZOPT, ZZ-SWAPOPT) to gates implemented with ECR-CX often yields better QAOA performance (higher approximation ratio and success probability) than using the improved monolithic direct-CX gates alone.

[supported] Direct-CX gates on ibmq ehningen have slightly lower average CX error (0.79% vs 0.83%) and substantially shorter execution time (256.89 ns vs 382.22 ns, a 32.79% reduction) than ECR-CX, per the collected calibration data.

[supported] Pulse-level optimization can substantially shorten schedules for certain two-qubit primitives: e.g., a ZZ gate implemented via ECR-CX could be reduced (ZZOPT) from ~640 ns to ~241.8 ns in the paper's examples.

[supported] Decomposing certain composite primitives (ZZ-SWAP) into pulse-optimized CZ-based implementations (ZZ-SWAPOPT) reduced gate counts/schedule length and improved algorithm-level metrics in experiments.

[supported] The hardware-native Control->Target polarity of CX gates matters: implementing undirected two-qubit primitives in the native CT direction yields better performance than using the reversed (TC) polarity.

[supported] Circuit fidelity (as computed from calibration data) alone is not always the best predictor of end-to-end algorithm performance; gate type and actual schedule duration must also be considered when mapping circuits to bipotent QPUs.

[supported] For dense QAOA problems (Portfolio Optimization, complete-graph MaxCut) transpiled to sparse hardware, SWAP gates contribute substantially to cost; pulse-level optimized SWAP/ZZ-SWAP primitives can significantly mitigate this cost.

[supported] A mapping strategy that trades off fidelity, schedule duration, and gate type (their 'Bipotent' mapping) outperformed mappings that optimized fidelity only ('Global') in many of the experimental cases reported.
[supported] Quantitative experimental AR improvements were observed from combinations of pulse optimizations and bipotent mapping (see 'performance_claims' for numbers).

[speculative] Selective calibration (calibrating only specific two-qubit links that are important for a given algorithm) could reduce overhead and further improve algorithm performance on multipotent/bipotent hardware.

[speculative] The pulse-level optimization strategies and decomposition choices explored are expected to generalize to other hardware-native two-qubit gate sets (e.g., tunable-coupler CZ or iSWAP architectures), but this generalization requires further study.
[speculative] Universal, fully automatic qubit-mapping methods that account for bipotent/multipotent gate-availability and schedule-duration trade-offs would be valuable future work.

[speculative] Combining these pulse- and mapping-level optimizations with selective calibration, error characterization, error correction and mitigation (e.g., dynamical decoupling, zero-noise extrapolation) should further improve performance, but the combined gains are not quantified in this work.
[speculative] Making pulse-level optimization available for all gate types (eliminating the need for extra calibrations) would likely improve usability and performance of bipotent architectures.
results_summary: This paper empirically studies QAOA implementations (Portfolio Optimization and dense MaxCut instances) on two IBM bipotent superconducting QPUs that expose two different CX implementations (direct-CX: lower raw error and shorter duration; ECR-CX: higher raw error but amenable to pulse-level optimization). Using pre-transpiled linear-swap-network QAOA circuits and multiple mapping strategies, the authors show that pulse-level optimized primitives (ZZOPT and ZZ-SWAPOPT) implemented on ECR-CX links often produce better end-to-end algorithm performance (higher approximation ratio and success probability) than relying solely on the apparently "better" direct-CX gates. They demonstrate that schedule duration and gate type (including native Control->Target polarity) are important predictors for algorithm performance and that a bipotent-aware mapping that trades off fidelity and schedule duration (Bipotent-ZZ-SWAPOPT) typically yields the best results in their experiments. The paper reports several quantitative improvements and recommends broader availability of pulse-level optimization and further work on automated mapping and selective calibration strategies.
performance_claims: Direct-CX average CX gate error 0.79% vs ECR-CX 0.83% (4.82% relative reduction in error for direct-CX) and direct-CX average gate time 256.89 ns vs ECR-CX 382.22 ns (32.79% reduction in duration) — empirical calibration data (Table I).

Example native schedules: direct-CX schedule reported as ~245.3 ns (example qubits [1,4]) vs ECR-CX ~320 ns (example qubits [1,0]); ZZ decompositions: direct-CX based ZZ ~490 ns, ECR-CX based ZZ ~640 ns, pulse-optimized ZZOPT reduced to ~241.8 ns (specific experimental instances reported in Sec. IIIC/IV).

ZZ-SWAP schedule examples: default implementations reported at ~992 ns (on some qubits) vs ~800 ns (other qubits); pulse-optimized ZZ-SWAPOPT implementations improved performance via CZOPT decomposition (Sec. IV).

In algorithmic benchmarks (QAOA-PortOpt and QAOA-MaxCut), the authors report that ECR-ZZ-SWAPOPT achieved up to 70% improvement in Approximation Ratio (AR), and on average 29% improvement, compared to Global-circuits at p=2 in one comparison; on ibm auckland Bipotent-ZZ-SWAPOPT improved AR up to 55%, on average 27% vs Bipotent-Default; and on ibmq ehningen Bipotent-ZZ-SWAPOPT improved AR up to 34%, on average 14% vs Global-B (these are empirical, per Sec. V C 1).

Reported simulated (noiseless) baselines for PortOpt: e.g., 5Q-QAOA noiseless AR values varied with depth p (Table III) — sample: 3Q AR ~0.993 at p=1 rising to 1.000 at p>=4; 5Q MaxCut noiseless AR ~0.914 at p=1 rising to ~0.997 at p>=3 (used as baselines).

Quantum process tomography (QPT) infidelity measurements for ZZ and ZZ-SWAP primitives showed that pulse-optimized implementations (ZZOPT, ZZ-SWAPOPT) achieved lower infidelities than default implementations and that CT (control-target native polarity) implementations outperformed TC (reversed) polarity in their QPT experiments (Fig. 8).
quantum_advantage_detail: The paper does not claim or demonstrate a quantum computational advantage over classical methods; it focuses on hardware/software co-design and empirical performance improvements of QAOA implementations on bipotent NISQ devices via pulse-level optimization and mapping strategies.
limitations: Study is limited to QAOA (Portfolio Optimization and MaxCut) and circuits with a high level of regularity, so results may not generalize to arbitrary quantum algorithms.
Experiments are performed on two IBM bipotent QPUs (ibmq ehningen and ibm auckland); conclusions may be platform-specific and not directly transferable to other hardware families.
Pulse-level optimizations considered are limited to primitives and frequent subcircuits (they do not perform full GRAPE-style compilation due to exponential compilation cost).
Pulse-level optimization was only available for ECR-CX gates without additional calibration; direct-CX pulse optimizations (which would require extra calibration) were not used.

Benchmarks are restricted to small/medium circuits (up to five qubits in the main comparative experiments) because of hardware topology and ECR-CX connectivity limits, limiting conclusions about larger-scale behavior.
The work does not implement selective calibration or additional gate calibrations in practice; it only uses optimizations that require no extra calibration.
Only readout error mitigation from Qiskit was applied; other error mitigation techniques (e.g., ZNE, more extensive dynamical decoupling) were discussed but not fully explored experimentally.
Qubit mapping used a pre-transpilation strategy on a linear topology (per Ref. [33]); mapping strategies for other topologies or fully automatic bipotent-aware mappers were not implemented.
Process characterization (e.g., QPT) used for fidelity benchmarking is resource intensive and was applied only to small gate instances, limiting the scope of detailed gate-level characterization.
Temporal coverage of calibration data is limited (hourly data collected in September 2022); device characteristics may vary outside that window and over longer timescales.
The paper focuses on CX/CZ/ZZ and ZZ-SWAP primitives; other two-qubit interactions (iSWAP, native gates on other platforms) were not experimentally evaluated.
[inferred] The observed advantage of pulse-level optimization over direct-CX might diminish or reverse as direct-CX pulse-level optimizations and calibrations become more widely available.
[inferred] The benefits reported (e.g., for ZZ-SWAPOPT) may depend on the specific noise profile and scheduling idiosyncrasies of the tested devices, so broader statistical validation is needed.
[inferred] The experiments do not incorporate or quantify overheads (time, operational complexity) associated with deploying pulse-level optimization at scale in production/financial workflows.
open_questions: How do the trade-offs between hardware-level improvements (e.g., improved monolithic gates) and algorithm-level/pulse-level optimizations manifest on other hardware families or future generations of devices?
To what extent do the paper's findings scale to larger circuits (more qubits and higher depth) and to instances with different connectivity (beyond the dense PortOpt/complete graphs)?
What is the quantitative impact of Control-Target polarity across a wider set of algorithms and devices, and how should transpilers best account for polarity during mapping?
How much could selective calibration of only some two-qubit gates (instead of calibrating all) improve overall algorithm performance in practice, and what are the cost/benefit trade-offs?
Can universal, fully automatic qubit-mapping algorithms be developed that simultaneously optimize fidelity, schedule duration, and gate-type (bipotent-aware) for arbitrary circuits?
How effective are other error-mitigation strategies (ZNE, dynamical decoupling, composite pulse shaping) when integrated with pulse-level optimized primitives on bipotent architectures?
What pulse shapes or decompositions are most resilient to the dominant noise processes on different bipotent or multipotent architectures?
How would the conclusions change if pulse-level optimization were made available for direct-CX gates (i.e., removing the current asymmetry in pulse-programmability)?

Are there algorithm classes beyond QAOA (e.g., chemistry VQEs, machine learning ansatze, subroutines in larger algorithms) that would benefit more or less from the bipotent/pulse-level trade-offs observed here?
How to best combine selective pulse-level calibration, error characterization, and error correction/mitigation in an operational workflow for financial services use cases?
future_work: Develop universal and fully automatic methods to map a given quantum circuit to a bipotent QPU, maximizing success probability and minimizing schedule duration.
Explore applicability of the proposed methods to other QPUs (e.g., Google’s Sycamore) and hardware-native gate sets (CZ, iSWAP, √iSWAP, Sycamore).
Combine the proposed optimization strategies with error characterization, selective calibration, error correction, and various error mitigation techniques (e.g., dynamical decoupling and ZNE).
Investigate resilience of different pulse shapes to noise to identify more robust pulse shapes that improve algorithm performance.
Implement and study selective calibration at the pulse level for specific qubit pairs rather than calibrating all two-qubit gates.
Work toward making pulse-level optimization available for all gate types, removing the current limitation that favors ECR-CX for user-level pulse optimizations.
Extend benchmarks to larger problem sizes, higher QAOA depths, and other algorithm families to validate the generality of the conclusions.
key_ideas: #idea:near-term-feasibility — Pulse-level optimizations (ECR-CX with ZZOPT / ZZ-SWAPOPT) on IBM superconducting QPUs often yield larger empirical performance gains for QAOA PortOpt and MaxCut instances than improvements from hardware-level direct-CX gates.

#idea:hybrid-approach — A hybrid workflow is used: variational angles optimized classically (COBYLA on QASM simulator) are deployed to hardware; mapping strategies (ECR-only, Direct-only, Global best-fidelity, and Bipotent) trade fidelity, gate type, and schedule duration to improve outcomes.

#idea:hybrid-approach — The proposed 'bipotent' qubit-mapping strategy selects linear topologies that include both ECR and direct links to balance process fidelity and schedule duration, improving QAOA results on small, dense instances.
#limitation:qubit-count — Experiments are limited to small problem sizes (3–5 qubits for PortOpt, 5 qubits for MaxCut), limiting conclusions about larger-scale performance.
#limitation:noise — Hardware noise and two-qubit gate infidelities remain significant; process tomography shows non-negligible infidelities that affect AR and SP despite pulse optimizations.
